previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of chronic pancreatitis, recurrent leg cellulitis, and asthma was readmitted with persistent malaise, shortness of breath, cough, and tachycardia following a recent pneumonia. She was found to have Strep viridans bacteremia, likely originating from a dental abscess in her right lower second bicuspid, which was confirmed on imaging and treated with tooth extraction. She was started on vancomycin, then transitioned to ceftriaxone after sensitivities confirmed susceptibility. Serial blood cultures cleared, and echocardiograms (TTE and TEE) showed no evidence of endocarditis. A PICC line was placed for outpatient IV antibiotic therapy. She also experienced transient atrial fibrillation attributed to infection, and nocturnal bradycardia with oxygen desaturation, prompting discharge on home oxygen at night and referral for a sleep study. Her reactive airway symptoms were managed with inhalers and benzonatate, and her diarrhea was deemed medication-related. She was discharged home with a plan for 14 days of IV ceftriaxone, follow-up with infectious disease, and outpatient evaluation for thyroid abnormality noted on imaging.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to the hospital for shortness of breath and 
increased swelling in your legs.  A number of tests were 
performed to make sure you were not having any problems with 
your heart or the blood vessels of your lungs.  Based on your 
EKG and lab tests for heart proteins, there was no evidence of 
any recent damage to your heart.  You were also sent for an 
ultrasound examination of your leg veins to make sure that a 
blood clot had not developed, since this can cause leg swelling. 
 No clots were seen in your leg veins, which was reassuring.

Listening to your lungs on admission, there was a significant 
amount of wheezing.  Your recent shortness of breath is most 
likely due to an asthma/COPD flare, possibly related to a minor 
infection.  You were started on a steroid taper with Prednisone 
and given nebulizer treatments to improve your breathing.  By 
the day of discharge, you were less short of breath and your 
lung exam was improving.  You should continue taking the 
steroids as prescribed, as well as your usual inhaler 
treatments.  You were also prescribed a course of the antibiotic 
Levofloxacin, which you should complete as directed.

START: Prednisone 40 mg daily for 2 days, then 20 mg daily for 
two days, then 10 mg daily for two days, then 5 mg daily for two 
days, completing the taper

START: Levofloxacin 750 mg by mouth daily for 3 more days (to 
complete a 5 day course started in the hospital)

You should temporarily stop taking your Minocycline until you 
finish the course of Levofloxacin.  You should restart the 
Minocycline once you have completed the Levofloxacin course.

HOLD: Minocycline 100 mg by mouth twice daily (restart after 
completing Levofloxacin course)

None of your other home medications were changed.  You should 
continue taking them as previously prescribed and as indicated 
on your discharge medication sheet.  Do not drive or operate 
machinery while taking Oxycodone or other medications which can 
impair your reaction time or make you sleepy.
